deep.reconstruction:
The page is printed text from an elementary textbook on proportion and practical mechanics: the end of §141 on carriage charges (Fuhrlohn) and §142, an Anmerkung with worked examples. On the right margin are cut-off handwritten fragments: 'Schw…', 'λ (1…', '(1-…', '× R…', '(1+…', '× R.'. These look like the start of infinite-product expressions, '(1 - …)(1 + …) × Rest', of the kind written out in full on the next manuscript page. There Gauss expands a lemniscatic-type function as a double product over integers m, n. The printed content is as follows.

§141.3: For equal load l and equal distance s, prices are proportional to road 'badness', p:q = W:w. W is the worse road and w the better one.

§141.4: Combining this with P:p = LS:ls from §141.2 gives P:q = LSW:lsw. So the price is proportional to load × distance × road factor. In practice the road factor is measured by the number of horses needed.

§142 Example 1 (equal roads): 6 Rthl buys transport of 9 Ctr over 20 Meilen. How many Ctr go 15 Meilen for 8 Rthl?
- Price per Meile: 6/20 and 8/15.
- At equal distance, price is proportional to load: (6/20):(8/15) = 9:x.
- Equivalently Ps:pS = L:l, i.e. 6·15 : 8·20 = 9 : x.
- Hence x = 20·8·9/(6·15) = 1440/90 = 16 Ctr.

Example 2: The same load needs 3 horses on a good road and 4 on a bad one. Find the price q for 16 Ctr over 15 Meilen on the bad road.
- Proportion: 9·20·3 : 16·15·4 = 6 : q.
- So q = 16·15·4·6/(9·20·3) = 5760/540 = 16·2/3 = 32/3 = 10⅔ Rthl.

Example 3 (begun): For faster transport use §140.3, Vmc = vMC (force proportional to mass × velocity). The text adds that human and animal speeds are bounded: a man unloaded manages at most about 6 Fuß per second (continued on the next printed page).

All of this is routine rule-of-three (compound proportion).
errors: Labeling inconsistency in the printed text. §141.3 defines W as the worse road and writes p:q = W:w. Example 2 instead assigns W = 3 horses to the good road and w = 4 to the bad road. Read as price proportional to the number of horses, the proportion P:q = LSW:lsw (with W = 3, w = 4) is consistent and the answer 10⅔ is right. Strictly, with q the bad-road price and p the good-road price, one should write q:p = W:w, so the text's p:q = W:w is inverted.

results.what: Compound proportion for carriage charges: price ∝ load × distance × road factor; worked examples giving 16 Ctr and 10⅔ Rthl
results.modern_name: Compound rule of three (Regeldetri / Kettensatz), direct proportionality

results.what: Momentum-type relation V:v = MC:mc for the force needed to move masses at given speeds
results.modern_name: Proportionality of impulse/force to mass × velocity (momentum)

results.what: Marginal fragments '(1-…', '(1+…', '× R…' consistent with infinite-product expansions of lemniscatic functions (continued on the next page)
results.modern_name: Product expansion of the lemniscatic sine / elliptic functions
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (unpublished, c. 1797–1800); Abel and Jacobi in print

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a printed elementary arithmetic textbook page with routine proportion problems. Gauss's marginal fragments are too truncated to read and appear to belong to the lemniscatic product expansions on the next page, which are already known to be Gauss's work.

checkable.asserts: The per-Meile price proportion gives the same answer

transcription_corrections: The previous page's transcription of §140.3 reads 'Vmc = vMc'. This page cites it as 'Vmc = vMC', which is the correct form.

The printed body text is transcribed accurately. The margin fragments are cut off at the page edge and are only partially legible; '× R' probably abbreviates a remainder or product ('Rest'/'Reihe'), but this is uncertain.
